title: Saga

validation.research: Six primary sources: Garcia-Molina and Salem’s original Sagas (1987) SIGMOD paper hosted by Cornell; Chris Richardson’s Saga catalog; Microsoft’s Saga and Compensating Transaction patterns; Temporal’s Saga documentation and Emily Fortuna’s compensating-actions article. The Princeton technical-report URL denied access; the original published paper was read through Cornell and no research blocker remains. The original long-lived-transaction motivation is distinguished from the modern distributed-service form. Sagas is retained as the original plural alias. Compensation, orchestration/choreography, uncertainty, lack of global isolation, progress durability, domain-specific order, and operating repair are explicit. Broad claims that independent databases universally preclude distributed transactions or that compensation restores the original world are not inferred.

runnable_example.verification: Exact demo output and trace T1/T2/T3 refusal/C2/C1 pause/C1 resume; pending compensation retains done=1, completed compensation is not rerun, and unrelated O99 remains held with four mugs available; terminal compensated calls are inert; successful forward completion invokes no compensation and is separately terminal; first/second-step refusal compensates only accepted earlier work; uncertain forward response after effect retries the same identity without double reservation or blind compensation; unavailable-before-effect pauses after one attempt and resumes on the same plan/state; compensation response lost after release can be retried without adding capacity; unexpected errors propagate without pretending recovery succeeded; repeated reserve/release, conflicting identity payload, closed-key late-request rejection, independent ledgers, and exact 1/1000 capacity/quantity boundaries. Trusted nonempty string operation keys and single-caller fixed-plan ownership are preconditions. In-memory sequential simulation only: no durable crash recovery, network, concurrency, transactional database, scheduler, or production idempotency retention is inferred.

example_limits: Original bounded sequential Python 3.11+ simulation of an orchestrated Saga. Each Pool models participant-local atomic reservation/release calls with separate ledgers, quantity/capacity range 1–1000, repeat-safe operations, conflicting identity rejection, and retained closed keys. Trusted nonempty application-generated string keys, fresh controlled state, one caller, and a fixed step plan are preconditions. A definitive Declined means no active forward effect for that identified operation; Unavailable retains the current operation for same-identity reconciliation/retry. O42 holds two of five mugs and one packing slot, while an unrelated O99 takes one mug. Carrier declines; Packing compensation succeeds; Inventory compensation pauses once and resumes, preserving O99 and leaving four mugs. Successful completion, earlier refusal, lost forward/compensation replies, unknown errors, late forwards, and boundaries are checked. No database, network, concurrent threads, durable journal, scheduler, process-crash recovery, authentication, production idempotency retention, or plan migration. Dictionary assignments model local transactions under sequential assumptions; they do not implement a production transaction protocol. The compensated state is not order fulfillment and does not restore global isolation.
publication: Local implementation only. No publishing, deployment, commit, push, or pull request.
